utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, Vladimir Santic, also known as "Vlado."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. I wonder whether the Prosecutor -- sorry. You have already finished with the witness -- whether the Defence counsel are ready to cross-examine the witness. Mr. Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I can notify you that the witness will be cross-examined by Madam Slokovic-Glumac, Mr. Radovic, and Mr. Susak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Akhavan. I don't know how to pronounce your name correctly. In examination-in-chief, we heard that you are a lawyer by profession. Is it correct you work for the Office of the Prosecutor? That's right. Regarding your work here, have you had an opportunity to see Sakib Ahmic's statements given to the Prosecution at a later time?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I have not seen these statements.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I have not seen these statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: While you were compiling your report on human rights for which you gathered data, as you told us during your examination-in-chief, how was the data analysed later on? Did you send it to Geneva? Did you work on preparing the report yourself in part? Could you tell us more about it, please?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: This was usually a cooperative effort between the field office, which was based in Zagreb, and the headquarters in Geneva. The field officers would always play a predominant role in analysing the information since they were situated on the ground and were most intimately familiar with the facts. The office in Geneva was largely responsible for editing and formatting the paper, the reports, so that it would be appropriate for submission to the Human Rights Commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Let me ask you about the text that we have here in front of us. Who wrote this text?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: This text was drafted in part by myself, in part by one or two of my colleagues in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Which part was drafted by you; can you recall? Are these the specific parts, or are there conclusions, or perhaps the introductory part? Can you tell us which part you drafted yourself?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Specifically, the parts which I drafted were paragraphs 9 through 12, on the town of Vitez, and paragraphs 13 to 25, on the village of Ahmici. The paragraphs on the city of Mostar were drafted by other staff, and generally speaking, the -- I'm sorry, paragraph 37, on arbitrary executions by Bosnian government forces in the Vitez area was also drafted by me. The conclusions were almost invariably those of the Special Rapporteur himself, Prime Minister Mazowiecki.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In other words, the portion which deals with specific incidents is what you actually drafted, the paragraphs which you just cited here; there were no other people involved? Did also ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat the name of the person?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did (redacted) also work on it?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. My colleague and I conducted the investigation together, so we gathered information. In certain meetings, we were together; in other meetings, we were separate. But the drafting of the actual report and its legal analysis was predominantly my responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: While you were analysing events and when meeting with people who were eyewitnesses to the events, did you use any notes or videotape, did you tape anything, or did you just take down notes?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: We took down notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you did not use any other means or equipment?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I am now focusing on paragraph number 17. You said that you personally drafted that part of the report.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That was based on the testimony of Sakib Ahmic whom my colleague, (redacted), had interviewed in Zenica on the day that I was interviewing Colonel Blaskic and Mr. Dario Kordic. So I was not present at that particular interview, but this reflects the information which my colleague (redacted) gathered from that witness, but this information was verified in a visit to Ahmici where we visited the home of the individual in question, and what we found there very accurately confirmed his testimony as to how many people had been present in that home, how many had been killed, the description of the house and the rooms and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You say that this description fully reflects what Sakib Ahmic told your colleague?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, to the best of our ability, this reflects his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: For the record, I would like to read this paragraph, and please tell me if it is accurate: "One eyewitness related how he had hidden behind a couch in one room as Croat HVO soldiers burst into the other. The family of the house were in the next room: a father, mother, four-year-old boy, and three-month-old infant. The witness heard a burst of machine gun fire and saw the husband and wife fall to the ground. The soldiers then poured petrol, which they carried in glass bottles, all over the rooms -- all over the rooms, including the couch behind which the witness was hiding. The house was then ignited with matches. The witness was unable to determine whether the family had been killed by the gunshots before being set on fire." Is this the report which was compiled upon your having interviewed Mr. Sakib Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, did (redacted) (redacted) interview Mr. Sakib Ahmic in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know this for certain, because from your statement my understanding is that you were in the centre in Zenica together where you interviewed a number of survivors of Ahmici, you mentioned 50 to 60 people. Then following that, (redacted) conducted an additional interview which concerned the exact location of the house, and you also said that another woman was with him, whom you believed to be his cousin. So from that I construed that you also conducted an interview with Mr. Sakib Ahmic. That is the first one. Can you recall this, please?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Firstly, I don't recall having mentioned anything about a woman being with him, whether his cousin or someone else. When my colleague, Thomas, went to Zenica on that day, I stayed in Vitez. When he came back, as we did every evening, we would share notes about the activities and interviews which we had conducted on that day. Thomas informed me that he had gone to the hospital, I believe, in Zenica, where he had interviewed an elderly gentleman who had been there for treatment of his burns. I recall Thomas mentioned that the name of the man was Sakib Ahmic, and that he had indicated the story as it is reflected in paragraph 17 and that we should go back to the village in order to confirm the veracity of his testimony. So I am quite certain that that is the person whom Thomas had interviewed in order to arrive at these conclusions. It is possible that he may have interviewed additional people who may have had some testimony with respect to the same home as well, but I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The conversations which you conducted in Zenica, where exactly were they conducted? Was this some kind of a refugee centre? How was this organised?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, there was what appeared to be a refugee centre. I believe it was in a building which may have been a cinema or something of that nature. These people had just been released, about 150 of them, from a school in Dubravica where they had been held after the attack on Ahmici. We found these people through a Centre for the Documentation of Genocide and War Crimes, I believe, which was an organisation in Zenica, but the interview was not prepared in advance. We simply went to Zenica, spoke to the representatives of that organisation, and they took us right there and then to that centre, and we had the opportunity to interview the witnesses without interference. Since my colleague, Thomas, had been a Serbo-Croatian translator, it was not necessary for us to have anyone else present.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In other words, you selected the people among those present; there was no organisation which guided you as to whom you were going to interview?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said that the people with whom you talked were, for the most part, children, women, and the elderly. Did you have an opportunity to speak to a male person of military age from Ahmici who could have been involved in the military?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: In that particular visit, no, I don't recall any such person.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were there such persons in this centre?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Among the group from Ahmici, no, we didn't see any such person. We were informed that the men of military age had not been released by the HVO, that only the women, children, and elderly had been released.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did the people with whom you talked mention the existence of the Territorial Defence in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did they mention any kind of armed resistance having taken place on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did they tell you that the fighting in Ahmici took two days and that only after two days a front-line was established above the village?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: We were informed that the fighting lasted approximately one day but not two.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who gave you this information?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: This information was gathered from several sources. We interviewed some of the witnesses who were survivors, we interviewed members of the British battalion, some of whom had arrived in the vicinity of Ahmici towards the latter part of April 16th, when the attack had taken place, and we were aware that certain people may have fled and hidden in the forest. If that is considered resistance, yes, it may have been that some of those people were not captured until after April the 16th. But in terms of the actual destruction and take-over of the village, our impression, based primarily on the testimony of members of the British battalion, was that on April 16th, a take-over and destruction had been completed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Given that in the report you mention that over 100 persons took part in the take-over of the village, would the information that you gathered lead you to believe that there was armed resistance in the village since it took a full day to capture it?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Firstly, I believe the number which was indicated in our report was at least 50 and possibly up to 150 soldiers. That is in paragraph 23. We came to that conclusion based on the information given to us by military experts, members of the British battalion, who suggested that the scale of the destruction in the village, the number of killings, the number of homes that had been set on fire, the use of mortar, so on and so forth, would not have been a small operation which could have been done, let's say, simply by a band of ruffians, that this was a concerted and organised military operation. We cannot come to specific numbers, but those are approximate numbers which I think were very realistic in view of the extent of destruction in the village. Now, what we mean by "military resistance" I think is a complex question. If we mean that someone who was in his home and saw that soldiers were coming to harm himself or his family, would pick up, let's say, a hunting rifle and try to defend himself, well then, it's possible that there may have been such resistance. But I don't think that in our mind that would have changed the character of the attack, that Ahmici was an undefended village, that there was no significant military presence or target which would have justified the attack; and that even hypothetically, had there been some sort of military presence, the scale of destruction was clearly disproportionate to any such military threat which may have been posed by that village. So it was on that basis that we disregarded the possibility of any serious resistance or, rather, the possibility that the resistance may have changed the character of the atrocities and their unlawfulness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether, during your fact-finding process, you also ascertained a number of victims on the Croatian side? Five Croatian soldiers were killed and nine wounded during the operation in Ahmici. Was that factored in during the preparation of your report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You put that, Mrs. Glumac. Is this a matter you are going to establish with evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, Your Honour, this will be part of our evidence which we will present. It is something that we are going to establish, and since we have an expert witness here, we have to try to bring that analysis to the foreground.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: We had approached the HVO authorities in the region; as I explained, we had spoken to Dario Kordic, Tihomir Blaskic, and Mario Cerkez. None of them had indicated to us that there were any serious HVO casualties in the Ahmici operation. We did understand that there were five Croatian casualties in the Vitez operation, and this is reflected in this report. I'm not certain if the five individuals you are speaking about may have been from Vitez rather than Ahmici. In Vitez, the Bosnian Muslim resistance was much more sustained than that in Ahmici where, as I said, the village was destroyed and taken over. Even two weeks after the events of April 16th, I believe in Stari Vitez, the Bosnian Muslims still controlled a part of the city, and in that case, the padre of the British battalion had indicated that five Croats had been buried along with 96 Muslims in the Vitez area. To the best of our sources, to the best of the ability which we had to get information from sources, there were no similar casualties on the Croatian side. The other casualties which we came across were in the hamlet of Miletici, where I believe between three to five young Croatian men had been attacked and beheaded by what appeared to be rogue elements. Those were the only casualties which we were aware of.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: If we take into account that we have five casualties and an additional nine wounded, would that change your view as is to the existence of armed resistance in Ahmici because we say that these are the victims from Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it would in no serious way change my view. The number of casualties in Ahmici -- actually, the number who were killed, were approximately 200. From what we recall at the time when we arrived, about 100 were confirmed dead, a large number of whom were women, children, elderly, many of whom were burnt alive in their homes, shot on their doorsteps, or executed by snipers in this so-called killing field in front of the Catholic cemetery. There were an approximately -- at that point, there were approximately 200 others unaccounted for, I'm sure many of whom were in hiding, but I believe that in the end, the result was that some 150 to 200 people, most of whom were civilians, were killed in that operation. I don't believe that five HVO soldiers killed with nine wounded, as a result of some sort of spontaneous resistance, would have changed the character of this unlawful attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor does not have a list of about 200 casualties. He operates with a figure of about 100 casualties, as far as Ahmici is concerned. So where do you get your numbers, please?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: When we arrived in the region, according to our sources, some 100 casualties had been confirmed because they had been identified and buried. The problem was that there were still many people buried under the rubble, many people who were burnt in their homes or many who were executed and left in the village. The British battalion had tried to identify and bury as many of these bodies as possible; but the fact, for example, that we found four bodies in the home of Sakib Ahmici is an indication that there were many other such bodies. We could even smell, if you like, corpses in the village. There was a stench even some two weeks after the attack which we detected. The problem was that many of the homes were booby-trapped, there was a possibility that there were mines or other dangers which would have made it an extremely costly and difficult operation to retrieve all the bodies. So we, having spoken to the International Red Cross, the U.N. High Commission for Refugees, and the witnesses, figured out that at that point in time, in addition to the 100 killed, there were some 200 people unaccounted for. Many of these people, as I said, could have been hiding somewhere and may have been recovered later, but based on some of the accounts which we heard from the witnesses, we estimated that there could be possibly up to an additional 100 people who had been killed but who were not yet located.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: But from these assumptions, have these facts actually been determined anywhere; in other words, has this number, which you mentioned, been determined positively anywhere?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, but for the purposes of the report, we did not claim that so many people had been killed. I will find the relevant part of the report. I believe it's -- it is paragraph 19. Of the 89 bodies which have been recovered from the village, most are those of elderly people, women, children, and infants. A list of 101 possible victims was obtained through the testimony of displaced persons who had witnessed killings. And towards the end of that paragraph, it is estimated that as many as 100 bodies may still remain under the rubble in the village, but items to retrieve them are very hazardous due to the instability of remaining walls. The village is described as stinking of death. I believe that there is another part of the report, paragraph 22, which says that approximately 300 of the original Muslim inhabitants of Ahmici have yet to be accounted for. So I believe that those paragraphs and the language which has been used very carefully indicates what our sources are, and there's no attempt to suggest that 100 people were actually killed, the language is, "As many as 100 bodies may still remain". But the fact was that of the bodies which were retrieved, there were very few, if any, which were men of fighting age. We do appreciate that there is a distinction, in general, in combat activities between killing armed men of fighting age and elderly people, women, children and infants, and that's why the possibility of some Croatian casualties would not, in any significant way, have changed our perception of events.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Another question related to the list of casualties. You said, in point 19, that it was 101 person who fell -- who were casualties in Ahmici. This is the official number you quote. You also say that in Vitez, point 9, you again mention the number of 101, 96 Muslims and 5 Croats. Is there a bit of a confusion? Because according to our data, a total of 101 was buried in the cemetery, from Vitez, Ahmici and the surrounding villages altogether. Is there a bit of a confusion here, because we are not aware of another hundred, because you used the same number in several points.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: We were told, once again by the padre of the British battalion who was involved as a religious man in such burial ceremonies, that there were 101 people buried in Vitez. It is possible that some of those bodies may have been brought from neighbouring villages. That we did not ascertain. In the case of Ahmici, we were told by members of the British battalion that they specifically recovered 89 bodies from that village, and a significant number of those bodies were in that field across from the Catholic cemetery which I mentioned. According to them there were 89 people. When we spoke to some of the survivors in Zenica, people began to give us their own accounts of having seen people killed, or not necessarily having seen people killed but realising someone whom they knew had been left behind and was probably dead. Based on those accounts, we indicate there had may be a list of 101 possible victims in addition to those which had been recovered.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So according to that, that is a total of 202, 101 in Vitez and 101 in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the 101 were possible victims. We could only verify 89, but we would consider those to be in addition to the 101 people who were buried in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Could you please tell us who gathered the corpses around the village? Was that the job of the UNPROFOR or the Civil Defence? You mentioned at one point that UNPROFOR recovered the bodies and then drove them back to Vitez. I mean the corpses from the village of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was informed that UNPROFOR had gathered many of these bodies. I had spoken with soldiers who had personally participated in putting the bodies into bags. My impression was most of the bodies were actually taken to Zenica where there was a morgue. There was one body, for example, of a family which apparently had been burnt alive in their basement, and this was broadcast on the television. That body, I understand, was taken to Zenica for an autopsy. So I'm not sure how many of those bodies were actually buried in Vitez, how many were taken to Zenica for autopsies and burials, especially because many of the survivors were in Zenica, and they would have wanted to have the burial at a location to which they would have access.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were the corpses of Sakib Ahmici's family buried? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, that occurred after we left the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You mentioned that under -- along the road there was a flat area which you refer to as the killing field. You mentioned 20 bodies were found there. Were they brought -- had they been brought there by someone from the UNPROFOR or people from the village, or were those people killed on the spot?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: According to what I was told, they were killed on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court where you get this information? Who gave you this information specifically? Could you identify the person?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I could not identify the specific individual, this is some five years ago, but they were members of the British battalion whom we had spoke with. We had very extensive discussions with anywhere from 15 to 20 members of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In which parts of the village? You mentioned in your report that you visited three locations, along the road, by the upper mosque and the lower mosque. Can you remember where the great number of empty shell cases were found?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were shell casings around virtually all the homes that had been destroyed, so I don't think they were concentrated in a particular part of the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: But you did not tour the entire village. You said you toured the part around the mosque, and then you later went to the upper part of Ahmici and back down towards the road. Those are different locations. Were the casings present in the Upper Ahmici, around the houses and elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they were. We toured several homes when we were in the village, not just one or two. We walked from home to home inspecting the damage, and we noticed that almost without exception there were many rounds of bullets around homes. In certain cases shell casings coming from anti-aircraft guns, in some cases shells coming from rocket-propelled grenades.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you hear from the refugees and the people who left their homes get the information that fighting began only after people left their homes? Did they tell you how they ran away, how they fled Ahmici and along which roads?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. The information which we received was that fighting erupted when most people were still sleeping, very early in the morning, somewhere around the time of the morning call to prayer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: But you're speaking about the part of Lower Ahmici, the place you identified clearly, around the lower mosque and the part of the road leading up to Upper Ahmici. Whereas Upper Ahmici is separated from the Lower Ahmici, as you have noticed, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes it is separated, but not such that I think there would have been a very big difference considering the attack. To the best of our knowledge, the attack was directed at the village as a whole, that the attack began with a mortar shelling towards the upper part of the village, forcing many people to flee to the south where many were killed by sniper bullets or otherwise harmed. Our impression was that the attack, as a whole, began very early in the morning, and that most people were completely caught by surprise. It may have been that some parts of the village were affected somewhat later, depending on where the attack began from, and that may have given those people a somewhat better opportunity to prepare themselves to escape, but that I'm not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were you told by interviewees from Zenica what were the paths of escape from the village?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Most of the people indicated the forests as being the best path of escape, and I believe there were forests towards the north of the village. Some suggested that the reason why the mortar shelling was towards the north of the village was to prevent people fleeing into those areas, and I believe that if my bearings are correct, also towards the east of the village there was a wood area where people could have fled.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: During your mandate when you visited the Lasva Valley, was it -- it was part of your mandate to establish human rights violations in the entire Lasva Valley, not only in Ahmici and Vitez, but in all the other areas, and also to establish human rights violations against Croats, Muslims and others alike. Did your mission accomplish both these tasks successfully?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, our mandate covered the entire territory of the former Yugoslavia. We were particularly responsible for the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. We had published, up to that point, as many as ten reports covering different incidents, different situations. It so happened at that time there was what we perceived as a Bosnian/Croat offensive against the Bosnian Muslim forces and population in the Lasva Valley region. We were concentrating, at that point in time, on the Vitez area. Subsequent submissions looked at other areas of the Lasva Valley. We interviewed all the sources, all the relevant sources which could have given us information, including the HVO authorities, and we did not come across information suggesting that there was anywhere in the Lasva Valley a victimisation of Bosnian/Croat civilians remotely approaching that which we had witnessed in Ahmici. The hamlet of Miletici is one example of the great efforts to which we went through to be impartial. Miletici was a very remote and inaccessible place. We even had problems approaching there by armoured personnel carrier, we had to walk quite a distance, but we ensured that we would equally cover atrocities which had been committed against Bosnian Croat civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: It says in the report that the incident in Miletici took place around the 16th, so it is possible that it took place on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I need to consult my notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Page 8.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It is possible. We were not sure about the exact date. Our impression was that it was a revenge killing. That was our impression.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You did not write that though?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. That was really not relevant. We -- in these reports, we are less interested in a sort of sequence of events, if you like, than in reporting atrocities which had been committed. The purpose of these reports is, firstly, to inform the International Community of events to try to provide objective sources of information about what is transpiring in that region, but also to try and pressure the respective authorities into respecting human rights. So the point which we had in paragraph 37, was to indicate that the Special Rapporteur was not going to close his eyes to atrocities against Bosnian Croats, or Bosnian Serbs for that matter, simply because the Bosnian Muslims were disproportionately victimised. That's why we went to great lengths in virtually every report also to include certain paragraphs on human rights violations committed by government forces. But this did not suggest that those violations were the equivalent of what had been committed by the other sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, you mention here the existence of Mujahedins. Did you really establish that they existed and were they involved in any way in the BiH army, in the parts about Miletici?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is based on the testimony of the Croat villagers which we spoke with. They -- of course, the term Mujahedin was used in a very loose fashion. Generally it would refer to elements which were foreign to Bosnia. Some of the villagers indicated to us that the people looked different and spoke a different language, which made us believe that they were mercenaries or others who were not from Bosnia itself. We were told that there was also one uniformed officer wearing the uniform of the Bosnian army, which, of course, was not uncommon. Virtually every man of fighting age was wearing a uniform. Also that there was some individual living in the lower part or in the vicinity of Miletici who was known for participating in criminal activities, in black marketing and so on and so forth. So the impression which we got is that it was a group of this so-called Mujahedin, together with one or two or three locals. It was not a large-scale operation, of course. It may have been something like eight to ten individuals who simply came in to what was a very small hamlet of maybe ten homes in order to kill a few people, steal some property and walk off.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: But you said that those people were beheaded and 27 people you mentioned in your statement, 27 Croats fled the village, so it was not an innocuous incident, was it?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Clearly beheading someone is never innocuous, but we are simply reflecting -- there is no hidden agenda, if you like, in this paragraph. It is a very accurate recollection of what we were told by the survivors. This is a -- I'm not sure what the motives of the perpetrators were, their motives could have been simply some sadistic gratification, or trying to get property from other people, but the effect clearly was to create such fear in the local population that they ended up leaving, which is not surprising at all. When we arrived there, there were very few people, mainly people who were so old that it was difficult for them to go anywhere else, who had chosen to remain. But we were also told by the local people that there was one individual who was wearing the Bosnian army uniform, and that usually they would be protected from such attacks, which were not organised military attacks but simply attacks of thugs, rogue criminal elements, but that on this occasion this individual had not protected them. They did not suggest, though, that this individual was the one who did the beheading, but simply that he had not stood in the way of those who had come into the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also mentioned in the conclusion that it was established that government forces, as it says here, paragraph 40, in the area of Zenica have performed several arbitrary executions, tortures, et cetera. And those were on days before your arrival to the Lasva Valley, and that in Zenica, at that time, 600 Croats were held captive. Wasn't that information alarming and didn't it require some additional investigation?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you're saying that this information is contained in the report or that it was an allegation?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: It is in the conclusions, paragraph 40?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. We did receive information that there had been some such incidents in Zenica. We did not receive information that they were committed on a large scale. Certainly not against 600 people. There was, clearly, a climate of violence, and fear, and terror in that region. The tensions were extremely high. There were on many occasions isolated incidents of killing or torture, and these, unfortunately, were quite frequent throughout Bosnia throughout the war. One of the problems which we have with limited resources in the context of such widespread human rights violations, is the task of selecting what we believe are the most egregious, the most serious violations. For us in the case of Zenica, there was no indication, no evidence whatsoever that there had been large-scale killings or even killings numbering in the tens, if you like. So we focused our attention on the events in the Vitez area, especially in Ahmici where there was very clear evidence of large-scale killings of civilians. So we, as I said, took great care in order to be impartial and to include, as well, allegations that some such isolated incidents had taken place, and to put the Bosnian government on notice that simply because the Bosnian Muslims had been disproportionately victimised that they would not -- that we would not overlook violations committed against others. But I don't think that it would be fair to say that the allegations of large scale atrocities against Bosnian Croats in Zenica were credible at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Will you please tell us, except for people from Ahmici, have you interviewed people of Croatian nationality from surrounding villages, concentrating on the Vitez area? I would mention Kruscice, Gacice, Poculice, Bukve. Villages from which Croats had fled and where tortures and murders took place. Have you interviewed such people?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: We made an attempt to approach some Croats, inhabitants of Ahmici, at which point two snipers, apparently from the HVO, tried to kill my colleague and I. That gave us the message that we weren't particularly welcome and clearly affected the rest of our mission, where we decided instead to focus on those who were in the Bosnian Croat leadership, who would have the best overall knowledge of what is transpiring in that area. This is why we met with Dario Kordic and Blaskic and Cerkez. We invited them to give us information, to give us explanations. And what was given us to is reflected in this report. You must follow that it was extremely difficult to move around that area, especially when the Bosnian Croats had indicated an intention to kill us. And indeed, even in Vitez we had to move in -- under heavy guard, in constant fear that a sniper or other person would try to kill us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You mentioned that Bosnian Croats attempted to kill you. From where did these sniper shots come? Did you see the soldier firing?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. These -- as we indicated in this report, Ahmici was clearly under the control of the HVO. There was little doubt about that, and it was only when we approached the elderly Croatian lady, who I believe was with two younger children, that the sniper fire began. Now, we ran back to the personnel carrier which was some distance away, and fortunately got there alive. We then had to base our information on what the members of the British battalion told us. The snipers were not located -- the fire was coming somewhere from the village, which was very difficult to discern.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: From which part of the village, could you tell us? From the north, the east, which exact part?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's very difficult to remember with exactitude. I could say that if my bearings are correct, it would have been roughly from the western part of the village, but it's very difficult to tell. One of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You had been warned that approximately a distance of 500 metres from the village there were frontlines. You have probably -- you had probably been told that when you were leaving for Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, we were not told that there were frontlines approximately 500 metres. I would have been surprised, considering the geography, topography of the region if the sniper would have been that far away. I think that the firing, according to the soldiers which were with us, would have come from the village itself. There was reason to believe that the local inhabitants were not interested. I shouldn't say the local inhabitants. Those remaining in the village were not interested in our presence. On a second occasion when, we went back to the region together with three European Community Ambassadors, once again a certain individual in the village came and made some threats to Colonel Stewart, and Colonel Stewart immediately asked to us leave the village. It was clear that the constant visits to the village were perceived as a threat by those Croats who were remaining in the village, many of whom were probably involved in the killings. That was what we surmised.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: During the time you spent in the Lasva Valley, did you go to Stari Vitez, Old Vitez?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What did you see there? Were there any fortifications, barricades, trenches in the part held by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Stari Vitez was fortified and defended.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you see and could you specify how many members of the BiH army were under arms?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Excuse me. The VH army?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: No, the Bosnian Croatian army, BiH?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't recall exact numbers, but there were clearly members of the Bosnian army there in uniform with various weapons. I would say that the weapons were generally somewhat primitive compared to those we saw elsewhere and I would also say that the fortifications in Stari Vitez were somewhat, if you like, of an island in the middle of an HVO sea in the sense that Stari Vitez was disconnected from other Bosnian Muslim-controlled territories. It was an enclave within Vitez, and I think that for the inhabitants of Stari Vitez, it was extremely difficult even to try to get food and to continue their life, because whenever they had to leave that area in order to obtain food they faced sniper fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was there any sniper activity from the Old Vitez towards the part of Vitez inhabited by Croats?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, actually, we did notice that some -- one particular individual was carrying a sniper gun, but whether that sniper gun was used against HVO soldiers or against civilians is something which we could not ascertain.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: During the preparation of your report, did you also talk to the members of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you say whether you talked about their presence in the Lasva River Valley, how were they organised, how many brigades there were, what was the military organisation there, where were their commands?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: This, once again, is very difficult to remember five years later, but what I recall is that the Bosnian Muslim military presence was largely on the front facing the Bosnian Serb army, that the Bosnian Serb army posed such a threat, and the Bosnian Muslim forces were so weak that they were not nearly as concerned about a potential Bosnian Croat offensive, or the scale of such an offensive. Of course, I believe that after the events of April 16th, that situation changed and significant Bosnian Muslim resources were poured into a counteroffensive against the Bosnian Croats. At that point in time, the Bosnian military presence was minimal, and it was largely outside of the Vitez area, from Zenica onwards. We toured the region, and we may have seen possibly one old tank belonging to the Bosnian army. That was maybe the extent of heavy weaponry which we had seen, possibly some artillery pieces, all of them at some distance away from Vitez, but we failed to see any significant or menacing Bosnian army presence in that region.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: This is a bit inconsistent. That means the weak forces, which you just talked about of the BiH army, and paragraph 9 in your report concerning the town of Vitez where you say that very little territory changed hands, even though the town of Vitez now is divided between the two forces and that most of the villages managed to defend themselves, and now you're saying that the resistance was minimal. In other words, that with the exception of Ahmici, all other villages managed to defend themselves, and even Vitez itself, that one part of Vitez, remained under the Bosnian control throughout the war. Can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sorry, how is this inconsistent? I'm trying to understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You just said that you ascertained that there were only minimal BiH army forces present in the Lasva River Valley, that most of them were defending the frontlines against the Bosnian Serbs. However, in the report, you say that the villages managed to defend themselves, including Old Vitez; and with the exception of Ahmici, no other village changed hands. This is what -- I quote you here. This is in paragraph 9. So don't you feel that there is some inconsistency between what you just stated here and what was written in the report?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it's very difficult to speak about territory changing hands when the population is mixed in the region. What we understood is that the HVO already controlled the Lasva Valley region, so in that sense, very little territory changed hands. The front-line, if you like, or the area of HVO control, did not change, but the Bosnian Muslim civilian population was eliminated. That we would not consider a change of territory in the sort of language which we would use in these reports. Now, we did not say, first of all, that the villages were successfully defended, we say that they were defended, that there was some resistance --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I say that it was not.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: That, I'm sorry, that --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: There was no change.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I'm only interested in the discrepancy between these two statements. You said that there was no change - you probably had demographic changes in mind - and that this front-line was established.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. "Very little territory seems to have changed" does not mean that the demography has not changed. Had we written this report after the Bosnian Muslim counteroffensive which came in the weeks which followed, then our report would have said that the frontlines have changed, that indeed the Bosnian Muslim forces have now taken over areas which were previously under HVO control. But, once again, we have indicated here that there was resistance. This does not mean that the resistance was between forces of equal power. On the contrary, our impression was that the Bosnian Muslims in that region were largely on the defensive. In terms of the dynamics of those attacks, our impression was that when one is engaging in a military offensive, the resources generally have to be larger than those of the other side which is engaging in a defensive posture. Some of the military people would tell us that the ratio between offence and defensive, in terms of resources, is usually 3 to 1; and certainly, when people are in a village, fighting for their lives and they understand that defeat means their execution or other unpleasant outcome, they are likely to resist to the very end. So indeed, in many cases, the resistance was very fierce. But this does not change the general pattern of what was transpiring in that region, which we believe was a campaign to try and eliminate the Bosnian Muslim population, to change the demography in order to consolidate HVO control over what was then to be Canton 10 in the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Just several additional questions. In your report, you said that you noticed in that region and in Bosnia overall that most people of fighting age did wear uniforms on both the Bosnian and Croatian side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In other words, this was some kind of a fashion almost in addition to being a widespread phenomenon; is this what you feel given the mass proportions of it?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not sure if calling it a fashion would be most accurate. I think that, at that time, all men of fighting men were mobilised, and it was understood that because of the severity of the conflict, that all able-bodied men were to participate in the war effort. This also included people who may not have been, let's say, very young. I also saw many people in their 40s and 50s were also donning uniforms, and I'm not sure what implications can be drawn from that in terms of whether these people were members of organised units or not. Although men wore uniforms and were carrying weapons, it seemed as if there was still a certain degree of order and stability. It was very clear who was really in control, but that's another discussion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: My last question: In your report, this is in D8, you conclude that the main communications line through Central Bosnia passes through the Lasva River Valley and that this region is of great strategic importance for both the BiH army and the Croatian army and that everybody was trying to establish control in this area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct. As I have described, we tried to provide the background to what may have been the source of the conflict, but then to make a sharp distinction between attempts to vie for control and atrocities committed against civilians. Our impression at that point was that the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna was increasingly trying to assert its independence from the Bosnian government -- for whatever reason, it's not important -- and that there had been isolated acts of violence. For example, I believe in Travnik, there had been a flag-raising ceremony shortly after the arrival of then Defence Minister Susak, and the raising of the Croatian flag had resulted in some violence, some shooting incident between HVO forces and Bosnian government forces. There were clearly a lot of tensions, and the Bosnian government had no intention of surrendering control over that area, which did not mean that they were engaged at that point in a large-scale military offensive, in large part because they may not have had the resources. But this is simply to explain that there were tensions in the region. The killings did not come out of nowhere. But it was clear, in this respect, that one side, in this case the HVO, had decided to vie for control of the area using the sort of methods which we saw in the village of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, when you state there -- you established that this communications line was passing through the village of Ahmici; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct. The road, we were told, was of strategic importance, and that was apparent.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac. Thank you. Mr. Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you were in Ahmici on the 1st or 2nd of January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: In May. I was in Ahmici on three occasions. I believe the --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Just the first time. I'm interested in the first time when you went there.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: That was the 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested whether your colleague, (redacted) (redacted), did talk to Sakib Ahmic immediately following your first visit to Ahmici when you went back to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I believe that the date of the visit must have been on the 5th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did your colleague tell you whether he was inquiring, and was this reflected in his notes, before he spoke to Sakib Ahmic, he had already talked to the local police?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Excuse me, that he had spoken to which local police?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: The Bosniak --

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: In Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do know that on the previous day, I believe on May the 4th, that we had spoken, not to the police, but to the representatives of the War Crimes Documentation Centre in Zenica, which I believe was associated with the government. I'm not sure how close a relationship it had. Whether on the following day, my colleague Thomas spoke to the police or not is something which I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But do you know whether Sakib Ahmic, before his conversation with Thomas, talked to the police, not with the Documentation Centre but with the former secret police, that is the State Security Services which was taken over from the former Yugoslavia by the Bosnian government and then later renamed?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: This I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. When you were compiling your report based on the notes of (redacted), do you know where those notes are right now? Are they still around? Have they been destroyed? Do you know what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not know where those notes are.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Where is (redacted) now? We are asking you what (redacted) said. (redacted) was directly involved, but we are not talking to him even though he was the one who interviewed Mr. Ahmic. Where is (redacted) now? What does he do now, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe he works with the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: He does, just as you do right now? Very well. You are a Canadian citizen, as far as I can see. Did you serve in the military there?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How do you know certain military details, for instance, such as that one side had certain primitive weapons whereas the other side had less primitive weapons?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it is the sort of knowledge which one acquires in such situations. We dealt a lot with military people throughout our stay in the former Yugoslavia, largely members of the United Nations protection force but also often the various belligerents, whether they were Bosnian Croats, Bosnian Serbs, or Bosnian Muslims. Very often we would have military manuals which would help us better understand the means which were devised for warfare since this knowledge was essential to our understanding; what constituted legitimate killing or destruction in the conduct of hostilities, and what constituted unlawful killing or targeting of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I asked one question and I got an answer to another one. What would constitute a primitive weapon to you, which you said was in possession of the Bosniaks and, let's say, unprimitive weapons which, as you said, were in possession of the Croats? What is a primitive weapon, what is an unprimitive weapon, according to you?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, let's say a hunting rifle as opposed to an AK-47 assault rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In addition to the hunting rifles, did Bosniaks also have automatic rifles, such as Kalashnikovs? Did you see those? Do you know what a Kalashnikov automatic rifle is? It was, I think, the most widespread in this area. Did the Bosniaks also have such Kalashnikov rifles?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: In the area of Vitez, did you see any tanks on the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I could go on for a while. I think that I have clearly stated my purpose through this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You said that when you were in Ahmici, that in some houses, you saw the local inhabitants; did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that the persons who were there were local inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: We were told that there had actually been a number of displaced persons who had come from other regions to Ahmici, so it is possible that they were not local in the strict sense of the word. What we were told is that those who remained in the villages and those homes which were not destroyed were those of the Croat inhabitants of the village, and I did not have an independent means of verifying this. This was the information which we received from the British battalion which I presume had intense familiarity with that region having spent six months patrolling the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So this is information passed on to you by the British battalion and not through contact with the local population. This is how you determined that these were the local inhabitants; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct. As I explained, the local population wasn't exactly eager to speak with us, although we made efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You related your personal experience when you were in Ahmici and you talked to an elderly Croatian woman with a couple of children or something. You said that you had been shot at. In addition to you being threatened by these shots, was the woman and those two children who were with her, were they also threatened?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Actually, no. It was very clear that the snipers were not interested in hitting the woman and the children. The only factor which saved us was the fact that the woman was interposed between us and the sniper. The first couple of bullets were coming from above our heads, which were clearly an attempt to get us into the open. Once we were into the open, then the sniper fire became much more direct, and it was very clear that once we were in the open, that they were trying to kill us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Was the elderly lady also scared by the bullets which were flying and did she also seek shelter at the time when you talked to her?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm certain she was scared of the bullets and she immediately walked away at that point, but there was no attempt to hit her. It was very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But wait a minute. How do you know, when a bullet comes whizzing past you, how can you say that it cannot hit her? You seem to be very certain of it.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Common sense. The possibility for the sniper to have hit the woman was very easy as she was standing in front of us. The possibility of the sniper to hit us would have been extremely difficult. It was clear that the direction of the bullet was coming from behind her. Once we were in the open, the bullets were no longer coming from some distance above our head but were directly targeted to us. So based on those observations, I would arrive at the conclusion that they were not interested in killing the lady.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How do you conclude that these bullets were aimed above you and not right at you? I would like to know what objective criteria you are using in reaching this conclusion so that this sniper did not aim at you. In other words, do you allow for the possibility that a sniper can also miss you when targeting you?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's possible that they could have missed. The objective criteria I'm using are sight and sound. The lady, the elderly lady, with the two children was standing in front of us. The sniper fire came from behind her. She, in effect, was blocking, I believe -- would have been blocking the sniper's view. It is possible to hear and even to see, in a very vague way perhaps, where the fire is coming from, and at that point in time, it was some distance above our head. Once we were out into the open and fleeing, then the bullets became increasingly close, and our impression was that the sniper would have had a very easy shot had he wanted to kill the elderly lady since she was standing still. Once we began running, it would have been somewhat more difficult to target us, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: If this Croatian woman stood in front of you, and the way you describe it, she was sort of a shield for you, why would the Croats shoot at an area where they could also have shot at a Croatian woman?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Our impression was that they did not want us in the village and clearly they did not want us speaking to anyone. When we approached the lady, we asked her whether she could tell us anything about what had happened on April the 16th and who may have been responsible. She was clearly very fearful of speaking with us and said that she did not know anything, she had not seen anything, and it was very soon after we began speaking with her that the sniper fire came. It would have -- on a balance of probabilities, one would say that that would have been an attempt to prevent us from obtaining further information from the local inhabitants for fear that someone may actually talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: In closing, let me ask you: I believe that somewhere you stated or wrote that you received information on persons who were -- some 18 names who were involved in the attack, and I think that you mentioned that 18 persons were identified as belonging to those who took part in the attack.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct. This was given to my colleague, (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: By which side? Who gave it to him?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: The survivors in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know approximately what date this was?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: At least a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I could use as accurate information as you can provide.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe it was on the 5th of May, the day when I stayed behind in Vitez and my colleague went to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know these names which were given to you, and were there, among them, the names that were provided by Sakib Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not aware what names appeared on that list, nor was it really of great interest for us to have the names of particular perpetrators. We were not involved in a criminal investigation. We were involved in preparing a human rights report which looks at overall accountability of parties to the conflict for humanitarian law violations. The fact that the survivors were willing to give us great detail, including names of specific perpetrators, helped us confirm the veracity of their story and the fact that indeed members of the HVO armed forces were involved in the attack on Ahmici. Those 18 names were of no particular interest to us at that point in time. They were given to the commission of experts which was established by the Security Council which, at that point, was tasked with gathering specific information about humanitarian law violations with a view to possible prosecutions in the case that a Tribunal, such as this one, would be established. I do not know whether the name of any of the particular accused present before us today was included in that list; however, I would not be surprised if it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Would you be surprised had that not been the case?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, you see, because we did not systematically interview each and every person. There were about 50 to 60 survivors out of a much larger population in Ahmici, so the names which we got would have been very random. It would have depended on whom we happened to interview on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in paragraph 17 of your report you described a conversation which your colleague (redacted) (redacted) had with Sakib Ahmic. Was this draft based on (redacted) notes of this interview and was this put into your report accurately?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, certainly it was put into our report accurately. It was based on the notes of (redacted) and it was based on the on-site visit to Ahmici the following day on May 6th, where we--

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm just interested in the conversation and whether it was reflected accurately in the report in paragraph 17. So I'm just interested in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: This is a question that has already been put by Mrs. Glumac. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm finished thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We decided we would not repeat the same question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I pay attention to that, and I thank you for this. I will -- I am finished. I just wanted to reconfirm this particular point regarding Sakib Ahmic, given his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Susak, have you got many questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to be very short this time because my colleagues have asked a number of questions. I have just two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: My name is Luko Susak, I'm a lawyer, attorney for Mr. Josipovic. In your report you stated that besides identified corpses, there remained another up to 100, which may have been under the rubble. You also mentioned it was hazardous to retrieve them because of the instability of the remaining walls.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: However, today you said that the bodies were not retrieved because the area was mined, the land around the buildings were booby-trapped. Would you explain the difference between that and what you said in the report?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: It may have been mined. I did not say that it was, but there was a high probability that there were mines or other explosives which would have posed a great risk. I also mentioned that in addition to that risk there was the problem of resources. It would have required a tremendous amount of resources to lift out of that rubble -- all of that rubble in order to search for dead bodies underneath, and since the British battalion was already stretched very thin as an interposition force between the two sides in a relatively wide area, they did not have the resources. I think the danger of collapsing roofs or walls was part of the difficulties associated -- part of the resource constraint which prevented such activities from taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Right. I just wanted to make a point that there is a difference between your report and your statement today. Another thing, you said that you wrote the report, you drafted the report, whereas the conclusions were written by Polish Prime Minister Mazowiecki, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Not only the conclusions but also the introduction and certain other parts of the report, especially those relating to the city of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is the area in Vitez. Were there any supplements or amendments made to your report before -- by a third party before the draft ever reached Mazowiecki?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: For the portions relating to Ahmici and Vitez, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that some additions and corrections have been made -- had been made to the report.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: The additions and corrections I mentioned were not maybe additions or corrections, but they were editing. There's an editing process where the office in Geneva would take reports or drafts which we have submitted to them and make the necessary changes in language, and structure and organisation of paragraphs in order to make it into a suitable format -- a format suitable for presentation to the Commission on Human Rights. But substantive editing of the facts I don't think was involved in that process.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You said that after adding certain facts and corrections the report was then forwarded on?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. The facts were not related to Ahmici/Vitez. As I explained, the parts of the report, for example, dealing with Mostar, were not prepared based on information which we had given the Geneva office, or information relating to the situation of human rights in other parts of the -- other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So those parts were included by the office in Geneva, but the information on Vitez and Ahmici came almost exclusively from the field staff. Geneva would not have had access to sources additional to those which we provided for the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You said today there were other reports submitted from the territory of the former Yugoslavia. You mentioned there were ten of them.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Approximately. I'm not sure at that point, but I think that would be a safe guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Have there been any additions or amendments to those reports, as was the case with your report?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I recall only one amendment being made to any of the reports that had to deal with the destruction of a mosque in Prijepolje, in Serbia Montenegro, where erroneous information had been received, and there was a core agendum in a subsequent report which indicated that that mosque in a particular town had actually not been destroyed but had been damaged. But on the whole, I don't recall any other such core agenda or amendments, and this is from roughly 20 reports over several years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And one more question. You said that you had arrived to the area of Vitez in order to establish to what extent human rights are observed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Would you please tell us what was your particular task? Which particular kind of human rights violations were you sent to establish?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the context of such violence, clearly the sort of violations which one would look at would not be, let's say, freedom of expression or freedom of assembly, but the right to life, cases of torture, cases of rape and sexual assault. In general, violations involving grievous bodily harm or death, in addition to, let's say, wanton destruction of property, which is an indication of discriminatory policy or act of persecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did you arrive with a plan previously made to deal only with human rights violations against Muslims, not Croats?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, we clearly did not. We only came with the LAN to look at violations in the Lasva Valley region, because that is where there had been a considerable amount of violence. At no time in this or any other investigation would we have such ethnic or religious preference in making our reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: All right. Are you aware that Serbs from the village of Tolovici had fled the area, and do you know who is now living there?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have no idea where this village is and what transpired there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Because there have been human rights violations against Serbs by the Muslims, by Bosniaks. Another thing; are you aware of the fact that Mazowiecki's reports sometimes differed from UNPROFOR's reports?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Do you give me some examples?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: I'm saying that because I found that out from the press, and I'm asking you if you are aware of this, because you had been employed at the centre -- at this centre at the time, because reports sometimes did not -- were not identical, Mazowiecki's reports and UNPROFOR's reports. You can answer with a"Yes" or"No".

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, what I can say is that the mandate of UNPROFOR was not to monitor human rights. Their mandate was to engage in peacekeeping, and where there was no peace to keep, to facilitate humanitarian relief. Now, it is conceivable that UNPROFOR may have had reports which differed in certain respects, because they came across information accidentally or incidental to the discharge of their primary mandate, which was not human rights monitoring. On the whole, we relied heavily on what UNPROFOR soldiers had witnessed, since they were one of the reliable sources and one of the sources which had intimate familiarity with the situation on the ground. But I am very interested to know if in addition to what the press has to say, and the press says many things without substantiating it, I would be interested to know if there was ever any serious contradiction on any serious matter between the reports of Tadeusz Mazowiecki and UNPROFOR. To the extent that there may have been a contradiction, I don't think "contradiction" is the right word. It could be that UNPROFOR was less interested in exposing atrocities than Prime Minister Mazowiecki was, and this is because of complicated factors which we need not get into here, but that is not a contradiction, in my eyes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, are you through with your questions? Because, actually, you said you would put two questions, but eventually --

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: I was just concluding. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we -- I don't know whether the Prosecutor is going to re-examine the witness. Let's us break now for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I only have a few questions following along the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, Mr. Radovic stated that you were of Canadian nationality. Did you note this information somewhere? Is this information found in the written report, the report from the Human Rights Commission, or did you give such information in the course of your various interviews or testimony?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Would the fact that you are of Canadian nationality be an obstacle to your activities?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would hardly think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, I would like for you to stand up and to approach the aerial photograph of Ahmici. Would you please show this Tribunal where you were located when shots were fired in your direction?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, we had -- the Scimitar armoured personnel carriers had been parked in the vicinity of the mosque with the destroyed minaret, so that would have been somewhere in this area (indicating). We had walked up this road and observed the elderly lady and her two children walking along a footpath, I believe, in this area. We should have approached her across this small field here. The sniper fire would have probably come from this direction here (indicating). There was a slightly wooded area here. The British battalion members believe that that would have been the most likely location for the sniper fire.
